lessons.title: TC39 Governance & Stage 0 through Stage 4 Proposal Pipelines
lessons.description: JavaScript evolves through a formal proposal process — understand how new features go from idea to standard.

sections.heading: TC39 proposal stages
list: Stage 0 — idea stage: just a strawperson proposal
Stage 1 — draft: formal proposal with examples and initial spec text
Stage 2 — candidate: complete spec text, experimental implementations
Stage 3 — candidate: spec is complete, implementations being built
Stage 4 — finished: ready for inclusion in the standard

codeExamples.heading: Stage progression example
explanation: TC39 is the committee that governs JavaScript's evolution.
Each stage requires demonstrated implementation and community feedback.
Stage 4 features are guaranteed to be in the next ECMAScript release.
Stage 3 features are implemented in engines but not yet standardized.

practice.task: Look up the current TC39 proposals at tc39.es. Find 3 proposals at Stage 3 or Stage 4 and explain what they do.
hints: Visit tc39.es/ecma262 for the main spec.
Look at tc39.es/proposals for active proposals.
Stage 4 proposals are the most likely to be available soon.

keyTakeaways: TC39 is the committee that governs JavaScript's evolution.
Proposals go through 5 stages: idea → draft → candidate → finished.
Stage 4 features are guaranteed to be in the next ECMAScript release.
Understanding the process helps you prepare for upcoming language features.
lessons.challenge: Track a Stage 2 proposal over 6 months and document its progress through the stages.

lessons.title: Explicit Resource Management (using/Disposal Keyword)
lessons.description: The 'using' keyword automatically cleans up resources when they go out of scope — like try/finally made automatic.

sections.heading: What is explicit resource management?
list: using resource = getResource() — declares a resource that auto-disposes
Automatically called when the variable goes out of scope

codeExamples.heading: using keyword basics
explanation: The 'using' keyword declares a resource that auto-disposes on scope exit.
The resource implements [Symbol.dispose]() for cleanup logic.
Disposal happens automatically — no need for try/finally.
await using handles async cleanup (e.g., closing database connections).

practice.task: Create a disposable resource class that logs 'acquired' on creation and 'released' on disposal. Use 'using' to verify automatic cleanup.
hints: Use using resource = new MyResource() inside a function.
Verify the cleanup log appears when the function ends.

keyTakeaways: The 'using' keyword automatically cleans up resources on scope exit.
await using handles async disposal for database connections and file handles.
This eliminates the need for manual try/finally cleanup patterns.
lessons.challenge: Build a database connection pool that uses 'using' to automatically return connections when done.

lessons.title: Modern Temporal API for Date/Time Operations
lessons.description: The Temporal API replaces the problematic Date object with a modern, immutable, timezone-aware date/time library.

sections.heading: Why Temporal?
list: Date is mutable and timezone-unaware — a source of countless bugs
Temporal is immutable — operations return new instances
Full timezone support with IANA timezone names
Built-in duration, calendar and range operations

codeExamples.heading: Temporal API basics
explanation: Temporal provides immutable date/time objects — no mutation bugs.
Full timezone support with IANA names (Asia/Kolkata, America/New_York).
Plain types (PlainDate, PlainTime) handle dates without timezones.
Duration objects represent spans of time for calculations.

practice.task: Using the Temporal API, calculate the number of days between two dates and convert a timestamp to a different timezone.

keyTakeaways: Temporal replaces Date with immutable, timezone-aware date/time objects.
Operations return new instances — no mutation bugs.
Full timezone support with IANA timezone names.
Duration, calendar and range operations are built-in.
lessons.challenge: Build a scheduling app that handles events across multiple timezones using the Temporal API.
